chapter: Traditional style, ragtime orchestra and closing questions
title: Street cries and Creole speech
summary: Wood recalls hardly any street cries and only a French-speaking family at Morrison's Cafeteria.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Well, let me see what else. I was going to ask you if you remember hearing any street cries.

I guess I do remember maybe somebody coming through selling strawberries uptown in the strawberry season. But, you know, it was an unusual thing. They were not a part of the scene when I was here in the 50s, at least of the scene that I was aware of.
If it was done, it was done in another neighborhood.
I was really wondering if you heard, also if you heard different things in different neighborhoods, but obviously not. Did anybody speak any Creole then?

Occasionally I remember, you know, you say Creole, I don't really know what you mean by that. I remember being, for instance, in the cafeteria line at Morrison's Cafeteria, and being behind a family of parents and a couple of little children, who were obviously New Orleans residents, and they were all conversing in French, and I found that, you know, caught my attention. But I don't remember a lot of that cultural side of New Orleans. I had no real reason to be into it.
